Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable Ivanti/Fortinet/SAP product version inventory (June 2026 advisory) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiSandbox WEB UI command injection attempt (CVE-2026-25089) · [LLM] Ivanti Sentry handleMessage endpoint RCE attempt (CVE-2026-10520) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Ivanti Sentry unauthenticated admin account creation (CVE-2026-10523)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
FortiSandbox WEB UI command injection attempt (CVE-2026-25089) AIExploitation High
Hunts for HTTP POST requests to FortiSandbox/FortiSandbox Cloud/PaaS WEB UI containing shell metacharacters or their URL-encoded equivalents, which is the exploitation shape of the CWE-78 command-injection flaw Fortinet patched in 5.0.6 / 4.4.9. The bug is pre-auth so the request will arrive without a valid session token. Rationale: Article names CVE-2026-25089 as a CWE-78 OS command injection in the FortiSandbox WEB UI exploitable via crafted HTTP requests. URL-encoded shell metacharacters (%3B=;, %7C=|, %60=`, %26%26=&&) are the canonical command-injection payload signature. Cross-checked Fortinet PSIRT advisory naming. Cross-checked against: • https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) probing FortiSandbox
  • Pen-test engagement against the appliance
  • Internal admin uploading filenames containing semicolons or pipes in legitimate form submissions
  • FortiManager automated config push containing escaped shell-style payloads in policy fields
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable", "Rapid7"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on SourceIP — is it an authorized scanner or an unexpected internal/external host? Check FortiSandbox version against patched 5.0.6/4.4.9. 2. Contain: if FortiSandbox is unpatched and SourceIP is unauthorized, block at network edge and isolate the appliance pending upgrade. Pull configuration to confirm no admin accounts were added and no scheduled tasks created. 3. Hunt: search outbound traffic from FortiSandbox to non-Fortinet IPs over the prior 30 days, review process activity and audit logs on the appliance for shell spawns, and confirm integrity of analysis-job results that may have been tampered with.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("fortisandbox", "FortiSandbox")
| where RemotePort in (443, 8080, 80)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has "FortiSandbox"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("%3B", "%7C", "%26%26", "%60", "&&", ";")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry handleMessage endpoint RCE attempt (CVE-2026-10520) AIExploitation High
Hunts for HTTP requests to the vulnerable Ivanti Sentry endpoint /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage that watchTowr Labs identified as the unauthenticated command-injection sink for CVE-2026-10520. Any pre-patch access to this URI is exploitation-shaped since the patch redirects unauthenticated requests to the login page. Rationale: watchTowr Labs (cited in article) identified the exact vulnerable URI '/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage' as the unauthenticated MICS-config sink calling handleExecute() backend. Article confirms the patch now redirects unauthenticated requests, so any pre-upgrade access to this path is the exploitation signature. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com • https://forums.ivanti.com/s/product-communication
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys/Nessus) probing the endpoint as part of CVE check
  • Authorized red-team engagement probing the URI after the article disclosure
  • Web crawler/bot indexing all known endpoints
  • Patch-validation script confirming redirect-to-login behavior after upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable", "Rapid7", "Burp"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the Sentry version via the appliance admin console — is it pre-R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1? Check if SourceIP is an authorized scanner. Look for 200 OK vs 302 redirect in response codes (200 indicates pre-patch vulnerable state). 2. Contain: if unpatched and SourceIP unauthorized, immediately apply the Ivanti fix or restrict /mics/api/v2/* at WAF; pull the Sentry config to enumerate admin accounts added in last 90 days. 3. Hunt: review outbound from the Sentry host for reverse shells, inspect process trees for shells spawned by the web tier, and pivot on SourceIP across other internet-facing Ivanti products for the same indicators of compromise.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL contains "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
(W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where csUriStem contains "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" | project TimeGenerated, cIP, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUserAgent)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry unauthenticated admin account creation (CVE-2026-10523) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for new administrative accounts created on Ivanti Sentry without a preceding authenticated admin session — the operational artifact of the CVE-2026-10523 authentication-bypass flaw that lets remote unauthenticated attackers create arbitrary admin accounts. Rationale: Article quotes that CVE-2026-10523 lets a remote unauthenticated attacker 'create arbitrary administrative accounts'. Audit-log surface for admin-create events without a preceding logon is the cleanest behavioural artifact of the bypass. Cross-checked against MITRE T1136.001. Cross-checked against: • https://forums.ivanti.com/s/product-communication • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136/001/
ATT&CKT1078 T1136.001
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT admin onboarding new Sentry administrators
  • Sentry HA cluster sync creating system/service accounts
  • MDM platform automation provisioning operator accounts
  • Tier-3 Ivanti support engineer creating debug accounts during incident response
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the audit log around the create event — was there a corresponding authenticated admin session within ±5min from a known admin source IP? If yes, likely legitimate. 2. Contain: if no preceding admin auth, immediately disable/remove the new account and rotate ALL Sentry admin credentials. Patch to R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1. 3. Hunt: review every admin action taken by the new account; pivot on the source IP across other Ivanti products; check for MDM policy changes or device wipe/unenroll operations that might be follow-on activity.

Vulnerable Ivanti/Fortinet/SAP product version inventory (June 2026 advisory) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory pivot identifying every asset still running pre-patch versions of FortiSandbox (4.4.0-4.4.8 / 5.0.0-5.0.5), Ivanti Sentry (pre R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1), or SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP / SAP Commerce Cloud affected by the seven critical CVEs disclosed on 2026-06-10. Used to prioritize emergency patching and feed the exploitation-detection rules above with known-vulnerable host lists. Rationale: Article enumerates 7 specific CVEs across Fortinet/Ivanti/SAP with explicit fixed-version thresholds (FortiSandbox 5.0.6+/4.4.9+, Ivanti Sentry R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1). Defender TVM and Splunk Vulnerabilities CIM both index by CveId, so this is a direct CVE-list pivot that prioritizes internet-facing assets first. Cross-checked against: • https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt • https://forums.ivanti.com/s/product-communication • https://support.sap.com/en/my-support/knowledge-base/security-notes-news.html
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1082
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Recently-patched assets where TVM data has not refreshed yet (up to 24h lag)
  • Decommissioned hosts still in inventory but powered off

Response runbook
1. Triage: rank results by IsInternetFacing=true, then by CVSS (start with CVE-2026-10520 CVSS 10.0 and CVE-2026-10523 CVSS 9.9 on Ivanti Sentry). Validate version data against the appliance admin console — TVM occasionally lags. 2. Contain: schedule emergency patch windows for internet-facing assets within 24h; restrict access via WAF/firewall ACL in the interim. 3. Hunt: cross-reference each unpatched host against the FortiSandbox-command-injection and Ivanti-Sentry-handleMessage detections in this article — if a vulnerable host shows ANY hit on those rules, treat as confirmed compromise pending IR.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245 crafted-file root command execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-auth crafted-file injection vector in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (vManage). Detects file uploads/transfers by SD-WAN Manager processes followed by root-context process spawns indicative of the improper-escaping primitive Cisco described. Rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2026-20245 in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager as 'improper encoding or escaping' enabling authenticated local root command execution via a crafted file. We pivot on SD-WAN Manager app processes spawning shell interpreters as root with shell-metacharacter cmdlines. Cross-checked against CISA KEV catalog and Cisco PSIRT advisory naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/publicationListing.x
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator-driven troubleshooting from CLI/SSH spawning bash as root
  • Scheduled maintenance scripts invoked by vManage upgrades
  • Backup automation calling tar/python under root
  • Cisco TAC remote sessions running diagnostic shell wrappers
  • Ansible/Terraform automation orchestrating vManage with su to root
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","upgrade","patch") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/log/","/var/backup/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process tree and the crafted-file path; compare the cmdline shell metacharacters against the article's CVE-2026-20245 vector and confirm the user is root via a non-interactive path. 2) Contain: isolate the vManage VM/host from the management plane, snapshot for forensics, rotate vManage credentials and admin API tokens; verify Cisco patch level. 3) Hunt: review SD-WAN Manager upload/import endpoints in access logs for crafted-file POSTs in the last 30 days, search for outbound connections from vManage host to non-corporate ASNs, audit recently-added local accounts on edge devices managed by this controller.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName has_any ("vmanage","sdwan","catalyst-sdwan")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","vmanage","vmanage.sh","confd","nms_server")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","perl","python","python3")
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(;|\||\$\(|`|&&|\|\||\bid\b|\bwhoami\b|/etc/shadow|/tmp/)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Computer has_any ("vmanage","sdwan","catalyst-sdwan")
| where ProcessName in~ ("sudo","su","audispd","auditd","sshd")
   or SyslogMessage has_any ("vmanage","confd","nms_server")
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(uid=0|root)\s.*(sh|bash|dash|python|perl)\s.*(;|\||\$\(|`|&&|\|\||/tmp/|/etc/shadow|whoami|\bid\b)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chrome V8 CVE-2026-11645 sandbox-escape child process from chrome.exe renderer AIExploitation High
Hunts post-exploitation of the Chrome V8 OOB read/write CVE-2026-11645. Detects chrome.exe (or msedge.exe) renderer spawning native LOLBins or shells, indicating either sandbox escape or initial-stage RCE following a crafted HTML page. Rationale: Article names CVE-2026-11645 as a Chrome V8 OOB R/W actively exploited in the wild via crafted HTML — the canonical post-exploitation tell is the renderer process spawning a non-browser child. Cross-checked against the Chrome Releases blog naming convention for V8 zero-day advisories and the CISA KEV addition. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/
ATT&CKT1189 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser extension launching protocol handler (e.g., 1Password CLI, mailto handlers)
  • Enterprise SSO helper spawning cmd.exe for cert enrollment
  • User clicking a .exe download and Chrome SmartScreen prompting via mshta
  • Corporate web-print utility invoking rundll32 for printer redirection
  • Webex/Teams native helpers spawning curl for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--utility-sub-type" and ProcessCommandLine has "smartscreen")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm Chrome major.minor version against Google's fixed-version advisory for CVE-2026-11645 — if pre-patch and renderer cmdline contains --type=renderer, treat as in-scope. Capture the URL history immediately preceding the child spawn. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or network containment, force-deploy the Chrome stable channel update, kill the chrome.exe tree. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for the visited site's IP/domain across the org, look for follow-on DeviceImageLoadEvents of unsigned DLLs in the chrome.exe address space, query DeviceProcessEvents for any tagged hosts running the same chrome.exe SHA256 to identify pre-patch population.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--type=renderer","--type=utility","--type=gpu-process")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\chrome.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\msedge.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\brave.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\mshta.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\regsvr32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\bitsadmin.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\certutil.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\wmic.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Arista EOS CVE-2026-7473 unexpected tunnel-protocol traffic to decap endpoints AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-7473 Arista EOS decapsulation flaw on 7020R/7280R/7500R series where VXLAN/GRE/decap-group endpoints will incorrectly process non-configured tunnel traffic. Detects tunneled packets arriving at a known decap IP with a protocol type that does not match the configured tunnel. Rationale: Article quotes Arista directly: 'the switch does not verify the tunnel protocol type, potentially leading to the unexpected processing of non-configured tunnel traffic' on VXLAN VTEP / GRE / decap-group endpoints (7020R/7280R/7500R). We anchor on traffic to the configured decap IP whose protocol is NOT the expected VXLAN(udp/4789), GRE(proto 47), IPIP or NVGRE — the exact behaviour Arista has refused to patch. Operators must populate the placeholder IPs with their inventory of configured tunnel endpoints. Cross-checked CISA KEV catalog entry for CVE-2026-7473. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices
ATT&CKT1599 T1599.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer test-traffic during VXLAN/GRE provisioning
  • Misconfigured monitoring probe sending ICMP/UDP to VTEP loopback IP
  • NetFlow exporter pointing at the decap IP for collection
  • Operator-driven traceroute probes hitting the tunnel endpoint
  • Legitimate multi-protocol services co-hosted on the decap IP (anti-pattern config but seen in lab/PoC)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination IP is a configured tunnel endpoint (VXLAN VTEP, GRE peer, or decap-group), correlate against the Arista 'show interface tunnel' inventory, and identify the source IP/ASN — internet-origin sources are the exploitation case. 2) Contain: apply Arista's recommended ACL mitigation upstream (or on the EOS device itself) to permit only legitimate tunnel protocols to the decap IP — per the article Arista will NOT patch CVE-2026-7473. 3) Hunt: sweep NetFlow for the prior 30 days for the same source-to-decap pattern, check whether any inner payloads were forwarded onto the L3 fabric, audit BGP/OSPF for any unexplained routes pointing at the decap address.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("<vxlan-vtep-ip>","<gre-endpoint-ip>","<decap-group-ip>")
| where not (Protocol == "Udp" and RemotePort == 4789)
| where not (Protocol == "Gre")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where HitCount > 1
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Arista"
| where DeviceProduct has "EOS" or DeviceProduct has_any ("7020R","7280R","7500R")
| where DestinationIP in ("<vxlan-vtep-ip>","<gre-endpoint-ip>","<decap-group-ip>")
| where not (ApplicationProtocol =~ "vxlan" or DestinationPort == 4789)
| where not (ApplicationProtocol =~ "gre")
| where not (ApplicationProtocol in~ ("ipip","nvgre"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, Message
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol
| where HitCount > 1
| order by LastSeen desc
(source:cisco-asa OR source:arista OR source:network) @network.destination.ip:(<vxlan-vtep-ip> OR <gre-endpoint-ip> OR <decap-group-ip>) -@network.protocol:(vxlan OR gre OR ipip OR nvgre) -@network.destination.port:4789
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^(<vxlan-vtep-ip>|<gre-endpoint-ip>|<decap-group-ip>)$/
| NOT Protocol=17 RemotePort=4789
| NOT Protocol=47
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, Protocol], function=count())
| count > 1
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, srcPort, dstPort, protocol, action, bytes
| filter dstAddr in ["<vxlan-vtep-ip>","<gre-endpoint-ip>","<decap-group-ip>"]
      and not (protocol = 17 and dstPort = 4789)
      and not (protocol = 47)
      and action = "ACCEPT"
| stats count(*) as hits, sum(bytes) as total_bytes by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, protocol
| sort hits desc

CISA KEV June 23 2026 patch-deadline exposure for CVE-2026-20245 / 11645 / 7473 AIReconnaissance High
Hunts orgwide exposure to the three CVEs CISA added to the KEV catalog with FCEB remediation deadline 2026-06-23. Surfaces unpatched Cisco SD-WAN Manager, Chrome, and Arista EOS instances using Defender TVM so the SOC can drive patching ahead of the deadline. Rationale: Article lists three specific CVEs added to CISA KEV with FCEB deadline 2026-06-23: CVE-2026-20245 (Cisco SD-WAN Manager), CVE-2026-11645 (Chrome V8), CVE-2026-7473 (Arista EOS). Defender TVM ships CveId directly so an exact-match lookup yields a clean exposure list, prioritised by IsInternetFacing. Cross-checked CISA KEV catalog entry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerability.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag: device patched but inventory not yet re-scanned
  • Chrome auto-update completed but browser not restarted
  • Air-gapped/management-VLAN hosts flagged as IsInternetFacing=false but still need patching
  • Compensating-control hosts (Arista with upstream ACL mitigation already applied)
  • Test/lab Cisco SD-WAN Manager instance intentionally left vulnerable for research
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort the result set by IsInternetFacing=true first — those are FCEB-deadline-critical. For each device confirm SoftwareVersion vs RecommendedSecurityUpdate; for Arista EOS confirm whether the upstream ACL mitigation is in place (since Arista will not patch). 2) Contain: drive ticketed patching with Chrome → enterprise auto-update channel, Cisco vManage → vendor-published fixed build, Arista → upstream ACL mitigation per article. 3) Hunt: pivot each affected DeviceId into DeviceNetworkEvents / DeviceProcessEvents for the last 30 days looking for the exploitation patterns in the sibling UCs of this article.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

go-base admin/auth endpoint access — CVE-2026-48031 exploitation indicator AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP traffic to the dhax/go-base CVE-2026-48031 high-value endpoints (/api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, /api/v1/token/refresh) bearing an Authorization: Bearer JWT header from a source that has never previously authenticated to the host. The article confirms forged HS256 tokens signed with the literal string 'random' will be accepted on every protected endpoint, so successful (HTTP 200) requests to admin-tier URIs from a new client IP are the cleanest exploitation telemetry available pre-patch. Rationale: All five matching URIs are the literal endpoints from the article's PoC (/api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, /api/v1/token/refresh). Successful (HTTP 200) responses confirm the forged token was accepted by the vulnerable jwtauth.New('HS256', ...) verifier. W3CIISLog uses Computer (its host column) instead of DeviceName.
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1606.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin user genuinely calling /api/v1/admin/users after authenticating via the password-less flow
  • Internal QA / smoke tests hitting /api/v1/me with valid tokens
  • Monitoring / synthetic probes against /api/v1/token/refresh with a service-account token
  • First successful login post-patch where the secret has been rotated but the same URI is hit
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","safari.exe") and RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the Authorization bearer JWT on the request and check the kid/alg/iss/exp claims; attempt verification with HMAC-SHA256 secret 'random' — if the signature validates, treat as confirmed forgery. Pull the client IP's prior 30-day history against this host. Step 2 (contain): Block the offending source IP at the WAF/CDN, force-rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET on the affected go-base instance (openssl rand -base64 32), redeploy, invalidate all outstanding refresh tokens, and require re-authentication. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the client IP across /api/v1/* to see what data was enumerated; review user-table reads, account modifications, and any token-refresh calls that issued new long-lived tokens; check git history for any other repos using 'AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random'.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (3000, 8080, 80, 443)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/admin/users","/api/v1/admin","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh","/api/v1/account")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let GoBasePaths = dynamic(["/api/v1/admin/users","/api/v1/admin","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh","/api/v1/account"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem has_any (GoBasePaths)
  | where scStatus == 200
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, Url=strcat(csUriStem, iif(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?", csUriQuery), "")), Method=csMethod, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent, User=csUserName, Source="W3CIISLog"
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (GoBasePaths)
  | where DeviceAction !~ "deny"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DestinationHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Url=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, Status=EventOutcome, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, User=SourceUserName, Source="CommonSecurityLog"
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any (GoBasePaths)
  | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Url, Method=HttpMethod, Status=HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, User=SrcUsername, Source="ImWebSession"
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hardcoded AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random pattern in dev.env / source artifacts AIWeaponization High
Hunts file writes or reads of dev.env (or any .env-family file) that contain the literal string 'AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random' — the exact template default shipped by github.com/dhax/go-base. Catches both ongoing developer copies of the vulnerable template into prod-bound repos/containers and historical artifacts on disk. Rationale: dev.env is named literally at article line 10 as the artifact carrying AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random. Catching its appearance on prod hosts or in CI artifacts flags every copy of the vulnerable boilerplate before exploitation. Content inspection (the AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random string) is best layered via secret-scanning, but file-name + go-base path is high-fidelity by itself.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers cloning go-base intentionally into a sandboxed lab
  • Legitimate CI step extracting an .env template before substitution
  • Backup / restore operations replaying a previously-cleaned dev.env
  • DevContainer / Codespaces provisioning that drops .env from a template
Suppression filter
| where TargetFilePath !has_any ("\\test\\","\\fixtures\\","\\sandbox\\","\\lab\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the file contents on disk (or in the artifact) for the literal string 'AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random' and confirm whether the host is running the dhax/go-base binary on an exposed port. Step 2 (contain): If the host serves traffic, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32-byte random value (openssl rand -base64 32), redeploy, and invalidate outstanding refresh tokens; remove dev.env from version control history (git filter-repo) and from container layers. Step 3 (hunt): Search source-code repositories, container registries, and S3 / blob artifact stores for the same string; correlate with UC1 to see if any forged-token traffic has already hit /api/v1/admin endpoints.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("dev.env",".env",".env.example",".env.dev",".env.local","app.env")
   or FolderPath has_any ("\\go-base\\","/go-base/","dhax")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("dev.env",".env",".env.example",".env.dev",".env.local","app.env")

Vulnerable github.com/dhax/go-base package present in software inventory — CVE-2026-48031 AIReconnaissance High
Asset-exposure hunt that matches DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities against the vulnerable go-base versions (anything prior to commit 0.0.0-20260517152733-cc82b9740fa6). Surfaces every host running the JWT-forge-vulnerable boilerplate so it can be patched before exploitation. Rationale: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities is the natural Defender/Sentinel pivot for CVE-based asset exposure. Matching on both CveId and SoftwareVendor=dhax + SoftwareName has 'go-base' catches inventories where CVE enrichment lags. Internet-facing flag elevates priority.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandboxed lab / training hosts running vulnerable go-base intentionally
  • Decommissioned hosts still in inventory but no longer serving
  • SBOM scanner that tags the vendored module without confirming the running binary
  • Forked copies of go-base where the JWT secret has already been replaced manually
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each matched host, confirm the go-base binary is actually serving traffic (check listening port 3000/8080) and whether AUTH_JWT_SECRET is still 'random' via a controlled probe. Step 2 (contain): Prioritise patching internet-facing hosts (IsInternetFacing == true); apply PR#31 (post-2026-05-17 master) or rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET out-of-band and add a startup gate refusing 'random'/'secret'/'changeme'/empty. Step 3 (hunt): Roll UC1 (admin-endpoint access) against the same DeviceId list back-in-time 30 days to scope possible prior exploitation; check for any new privileged AAD/IAM accounts created during the window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-48031"
   or (SoftwareVendor =~ "dhax" and SoftwareName has "go-base")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, OSPlatform
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc

   or (SoftwareVendor =~ "dhax" and SoftwareName has "go-base")

    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId

  ) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc

JWT bearer token with extreme far-future expiration to go-base endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Authorization: Bearer JWTs sent to dhax/go-base endpoints whose decoded exp claim is more than 1 year beyond the request time — the article's PoC sets exp=9999999999 (year 2286), a near-pathognomonic forge signature. Pairs the URI from UC1 with a content-of-JWT predicate captured by the reverse proxy / API gateway. Rationale: The PoC at the article sets exp=9999999999 and iat=9999999000 — any production go-base token issued with the patched code uses minute-to-hour lifetimes, so exp > now+365d on a successful /api/v1/* request is a high-fidelity forge indicator. Sentinel KQL decodes the JWT payload inline; Defender DeviceNetworkEvents lacks header inspection so the runbook routes analysts to the proxy log.
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate long-lived service-account tokens issued for machine-to-machine integrations (rare in go-base but possible)
  • CI / synthetic monitoring tokens deliberately minted with year+ exp
  • Test tokens left in staging by developers
  • Misconfigured token lifetime policy on the application itself (legit but worth flagging)
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and Sub !has_any ("healthcheck","synthetic-probe","ci-runner")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Verify the bearer token signature against HS256 secret 'random' — if it validates, the token is forged. Compare the decoded sub/roles claim against IdentityInfo for the same user. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET on the affected host, invalidate all refresh tokens, and force re-authentication for every active session. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP across all /api/v1/* URIs over the last 30 days; review admin-tier responses for data egress; check if any new IAM/AAD principals were created during the window; verify the host has been patched per PR#31.
// Defender does not decode JWT payloads; emit the URI hit and let the analyst inspect the captured Authorization header at the proxy.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/admin","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","safari.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
Domainso4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock pinning compromised onering 1.4.1
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to onering crate's Sentry-disguised C2 ingest endpoint · [LLM] Rust build-script-build-*.exe initiating outbound public network connection · [LLM] Curl invoked from Rust build context with Sentry envelope Content-Type header · [LLM] Sentry envelope POST payload pattern in proxy / HTTP capture · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cargo build script invoking git log --pretty=format JSON and git diff HEAD^ HEAD · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Outbound connection to onering crate's Sentry-disguised C2 ingest endpoint AICommand & Control High
Hunts for any host contacting the attacker-controlled Sentry ingest URL hard-coded in onering 1.4.1's malicious build.rs. The DSN and org/project IDs are fixed strings in the payload, making this a pinpoint IOC pivot. Rationale: Article hard-codes DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821, org id o4511539639222272, and project id 4511539669368912. Any traffic to this Sentry tenant from infrastructure that has not opted into this DSN is malicious by definition. Validated against the maintainer-disclosure GitHub issue cited in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Sentry SDK integration accidentally using the same tenant (extremely unlikely — different org id)
  • Security researcher reproducing the IOC in a sandbox
  • Proxy/SIEM log replay during detection tuning
  • Threat-intel feed validation traffic
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source process and pull its tree (curl invoked by build-script-build-*.exe from a cargo target/debug directory). Capture the Cargo.lock to confirm onering 1.4.1 is pinned. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the developer/CI host, kill cargo/rustc, block the Sentry DSN domain at egress, and revoke any credentials the user touched in the last 24h since git diffs may have exfiltrated secrets-in-code. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every host with onering 1.4.1 in any Cargo.lock or ~/.cargo/registry/cache, audit all git commits pushed since the build, and assume the latest commit diff content is attacker-known.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
   or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
   or Url has "4511539669368912/envelope"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust build-script-build-*.exe initiating outbound public network connection AICommand & Control High
Cargo compiles each crate's build.rs into a transient binary named build-script-build-<hash>.exe. These should never reach the public internet — the onering malicious build script does exactly this. Rationale: Article states the malicious build.rs uses curl via Rust's request() function. Cargo always emits build scripts as build-script-build-<hash>.exe under target/debug/build/ — that path + outbound public traffic is near-zero noise. Sentinel uses 4688 process creation since ImNetworkSession lacks process attribution; pivot to firewall logs in triage.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crates that legitimately fetch resources at build time (e.g. libtorch-sys downloading binaries — anti-pattern but exists)
  • openssl-src or bindgen pulling submodules
  • CI pre-warmed cargo registries refreshing
  • Developer running `cargo build` behind authenticated proxy logs as build script egress
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "openssl-src" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "bindgen"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enumerate the Cargo.lock in the host's project tree and identify which crate produced the build-script-build binary (hash maps to crate via cargo metadata). Step 2 — Contain: kill the build, block egress, and preserve the build-script-build-*.exe + the source crate's build.rs. Step 3 — Hunt: check for the specific onering 1.4.1 IOC and any other crates with build.rs invoking curl/wget/reqwest/ureq from across the fleet's Cargo.lock files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "build-script-build"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cargo.exe","rustc.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\target\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\build-script-build-[a-f0-9]+\.exe$"
   or NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\build-script-build\.exe$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cargo.exe","rustc.exe")
   or NewProcessName has @"\target\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cargo build script invoking git log --pretty=format JSON and git diff HEAD^ HEAD AIActions on Objectives High
The onering 1.4.1 build.rs executes two very specific git commands to harvest commit metadata and the latest patch. The --pretty=format string and the HEAD^ HEAD diff pair are fingerprintable on the command line. Rationale: Verbatim from the article's leaked source: the build.rs uses --pretty=format:{"commit":"%H","author":"%an","email":"%ae","date":"%aI","subject":"%s"} and git diff HEAD^ HEAD. The combined token set of all five JSON keys is unique to this attacker. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1005 T1213.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bespoke developer scripts that export commit metadata to JSON for changelog generation
  • GitHub Actions workflows using git log --pretty=format for release notes (typically don't use all five fields)
  • CI pipelines generating semantic-versioning manifests
  • git-cliff or similar conventional-commits tools
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git-cliff.exe","semantic-release.exe","conventional-changelog.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: dump the full process tree; expect cargo.exe → build-script-build-*.exe → git.exe with these args. Step 2 — Contain: kill the cargo session, snapshot Cargo.lock, and quarantine the build-script-build binary. Step 3 — Hunt: assume the entire last commit diff was exfiltrated; pull the diff and treat any secret-shaped strings (tokens, keys, passwords) as compromised; sweep other developer machines for onering in Cargo.lock.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "git.exe" or FileName =~ "git"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("--pretty=format","commit","author","email","date","subject")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "diff HEAD^ HEAD"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)diff\s+HEAD\^\s+HEAD"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "build-script-build"
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cargo.exe","rustc.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\target\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "git.exe" or ActingProcessName =~ "git" or TargetProcessName =~ "git.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("--pretty=format","commit","author","email","date")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)diff\s+HEAD\^\s+HEAD"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_all ("--pretty=format","commit","author","email","date")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)diff\s+HEAD\^\s+HEAD"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cargo.exe","rustc.exe","build-script-build")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Curl invoked from Rust build context with Sentry envelope Content-Type header AICommand & Control High
The onering build.rs POSTs the stolen diff as a fake Sentry envelope using Content-Type: application/x-sentry-envelope. That header in a curl process whose parent is cargo/rustc/build-script-build is highly anomalous. Rationale: Article quotes the literal HTTP header Content-Type: application/x-sentry-envelope in the payload's request() call. Real Sentry SDKs almost never shell out to curl with this header — observing it on a developer/CI host is a high-fidelity exfiltration indicator.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke shell script that wraps the Sentry envelope API for crash uploads
  • Sentry self-host migration tooling
  • Pentest tooling reproducing the IOC for purple-team exercises
  • Security awareness training reenactment
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the full curl command line; check the destination URL against the onering Sentry DSN IOC. Step 2 — Contain: kill the build, block egress, preserve the parent build-script-build binary and any cargo target/ directory, quarantine the host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the curl parent to find the dependent project; pull Cargo.lock for the same crate version from every other host; rotate any secrets the latest commit touched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe" or FileName =~ "curl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-sentry-envelope"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "application/x-sentry-envelope"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/envelope/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "curl.exe" or ActingProcessName =~ "curl" or TargetProcessName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-sentry-envelope"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "x-sentry-envelope"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "/envelope/"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/envelope/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Curl With Sentry Envelope Content-Type Used For Source Code Exfiltration
